cukrga:237: SkillClaw reveals a fundamental contradiction in current Agent skill systems: skills remain basically static after deployment, while users continuously generate improvement signals during real-world use. The essence of this contradiction is the one-way nature of knowledge flow—improvements remain only in the current session and cannot be passed to the skill library or other users. SkillClaw's approach is to treat multi-user interactions as a "natural ablation experiment" on skill behavior: the success/failure patterns generated when different users invoke the same skill in different scenarios constitute empirical evidence of the skill's behavioral boundaries. This means data from a single user is insufficient to distinguish "general improvement" from "case-specific fix", but once multi-user evidence is aggregated, a stable evolutionary direction emerges.

o2j6yj:290: The core of SkillClaw is the Agentic Evolver—an LLM Agent equipped with a structured Harness, responsible for open-ended reasoning updates to the shared skill library. Given a skill and its session groups, the Evolver performs three operations: Refine (refines the skill based on failure patterns), Create (creates a new skill when uncovered reusable sub-processes are found), Skip (keeps unchanged when evidence is insufficient). The key design is that the Evolver always jointly analyzes success and failure sessions—success sessions define "invariants" (the valid parts that must be preserved), failure sessions define "targets" (the specific behaviors to be fixed). This joint analysis prevents the common failure mode of "fixing one bug and introducing three new bugs", and is the core mechanism that distinguishes SkillClaw from simple rule-based fixes.
oe5a7a:218: Nightly validation is the key mechanism SkillClaw uses to ensure monotonic deployment behavior. Evolved candidate skills are not directly deployed; instead, they enter the nightly validation stage: the old skill and the new candidate skill are executed concurrently in a real environment, comparing overall task success rate and execution stability. The new skill is accepted only if it is genuinely better than the old one. This guarantees that the deployed skill pool does not degrade over time—users always interact with "the best skill pool validated the previous night".
